newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW-Asia seen needing corporate restructurin.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Asia seen needing corporate restructurin.

text.p: Asia's problems are more corporate than economic and an entirely new approach is needed to fix them, Dresdner Kleinwort Benson (DKB) said in a research report.
"The key to a recovery is to have better corporates. This will take longer than the normal cyclical turnaround," DKB said.
Despite different economic structures, similar symptoms of Asia's sputtering economic growth engine have emerged in countries throughout the region.

Falling productivity rates, severe bouts of asset price inflation, slowing export growth rates, growing imports and rising cost pressures are signs that government policies are out of date and that corporate attitudes must change.
"The current economic woes will not go away unless there is a definitive change in corporate attitudes. Asia needs to revamp its business plan, not tinker with its economic policies," DKB said.
The root of Asia's economic malaise was its failure to recognise the limits of government "diktat", the brokerage said.

Asia's economic "miracle" has depended largely upon active government intervention. Governments prevailed upon people to save rather than spend, keeping wages low while countries built beachheads in export markets in developed economies.

Cheap credit was extended to industry, enhancing export competitiveness through cheap currencies and protection of domestic industry. This created an informal, implicit system of price controls and credit guidelines which distorted demand patterns and capital allocation, DKB said.
But once full employment was reached, the consequences of such arbitrary economic management started to surface.

Governments that resisted the natural replacement of the manufacturing sector by the services sector started to see manufacturing rates of return decline while accumulated wealth found its way into assets, spurring asset price inflation.
Reluctance to change a winning game-plan saw governments persist with out-dated policies, such as pouring capital into "desirable" industries.
"The banking system is usually asked to go along. Not surprisingly, some Asian tigers now face banking and balance of payments problems," DKB said.

Asian companies now face a variety of challenges. Consumers have become more discriminating, demanding higher-quality goods, while saturated markets are preventing companies from growing their way out of problems, as in the past.
Smart workers are becoming harder to retain, investors have greater choice and the Asian model of family ownership is turning into a management headache in larger corporations.

The widespread corporate restructuring now on the cards was likely to turn into a "gut-wrenching" process, DKB warned. "Quite clearly, there will be much foot-dragging because allowing market forces to work will typically stir up a hornet's nest of vested interests. But the economic costs of sustaining economically franchised beneficiaries will rise to a point of negative returns. The usual wake-up call is a banking crisis."
The next stage of the Asian growth story would see diverging corporate performance as competition produced winners and losers, DKB said.
"Local conglomerates must now contemplate downsizing to be compatible with market demand and to improve financial and management efficiency."
